utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, your next witness is?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next witness is Branko Fezer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Fezer. Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You'll now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, before we start our examination-in-chief, is it true that you made a statement to the Ojdanic Defence team on the 3rd of September, 1997 [as interpreted], this statement was recorded and you signed it, did you not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Upon your arrival in The Hague, did you look at that statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Were you to testify before this Trial Chamber, would you answer all the questions from the statement in the same way?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we would like to tender the witness's statement under Rule 92 ter, the statement bears the following number: 3D1118.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In your statement you provided a detail account of your background and your duties. Can you just tell the Trial Chamber in 1998 and 1999 what post did you hold?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Throughout that time, I held the post of deputy head of the personnel administration. I was also in charge of the general cadre in the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In the second half of November 1998 there was a change in the position of the Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything more about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: As for that particular replacement at the very top of the General Staff, I can tell you this, sometime in mid-November 1998 a non-commissioned officer came over from the military cabinet of the president himself, he was authorised to request information on certain generals and admirals, about a dozen of them, who were then on duty. I prepared those, I gave them to the officer, and he took this back. I'm not sure when he did this. Several days later in the press, in the media, it was published that a meeting of the Supreme Defence Council had been held, that at this meeting the decision was taken to appoint General Ojdanic new deputy of the General Staff and that General Perisic who had been Chief of the General Staff up to that point would now become advisor to the president -- deputy prime minister, and then the handover took place between General Ojdanic and Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown Exhibit P796.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you see the document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber what this document is about and where is it kept?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: This is exactly what normally happens when there is a handover at any level of command. It comprises the fundamental procedure. You see the signatures of both the person taking over and the person handing over. The handover took place pursuant to a decision of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, according to his decree. This is kept in the files of both the person taking over and the person handing over, and each of them kept a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Following the appointment of General Ojdanic as Chief of the General Staff, there were certain personnel reshuffles in the General Staff, weren't there? Can you tell us about the most important changes that took place and what the reasons were?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: The most important changes occurred at the very top of the General Staff. Ojdanic was appointed Chief of the General Staff and this left the position of the deputy chief vacant. This position had been held by General Ojdanic previously, of course. Certain possibilities, certain options were considered, certain officers were considered who might be appointed. The proposal was made for General Marjanovic to be appointed, his name was put forward; he had been the chief of inspection of the VJ and the army's chief inspector at the same time. In the course of this reshuffle, the position left vacant was the position of the chief inspector, which was a very important position. And then possibility was considered that another officer should be appointed, and then General Samardzic's name came up, who was then commander of the 3rd Army. If the president and the Supreme Council accepted this proposal, this would have left vacant the position of commander of the 3rd Army. So the proposal was made that General Pavkovic should be appointed to that position, and he had previously been commander of the Pristina Corps. So what happened is that the position of the Pristina Corps commander was left vacant and the previous Chief of Staff, General Lazarevic, was proposed as the new commander. This was all phrased as a proposal. As soon as it was put together and as soon as all the arguments were put forward, this was submitted to the Supreme Defence Council for review [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now look at 3D731, it's a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, there is an addition to the transcript on page 4, line 24, the witness said: It was submitted to the Supreme Defence Council for review, in fact to the president, I mean maybe it can be established by hearing the tape, but it doesn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's helpful clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what we have before us is not the original document. This was -- this is a diagram that is based on General Fezer's statement. We'll use it for what it is, it is a diagram. It is just meant to illustrate what General Fezer is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you please explain what this is about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we've got the picture, Mr. Visnjic, unless there's some twist along the way, then I don't know that you need to go into this in any more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in paragraph 6 of your statement you describe a number of personnel changes that were made in the VJ, and based on the documents that we have I will be asking you a number of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have P797.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you're about to see a note on the handover between General Velickovic and General Grahovac. Can you tell us what you know about this particular change, when it occurred and what you believe were the reasons for it were.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: This came about at a later stage, sometime in March I think or perhaps later than that. As to the reasons, I don't know the reasons, because the personnel administration, the body of which I was in charge, is a technical body. We transformed decisions into appropriate documents. I did not know the reasons for these changes. I knew that a decision had been taken, and we were to draft the appropriate document for review by the relevant officer, in this case the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another document, P804.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Another note or report on the handover between General Panic, assistant Chief of the General Staff for the ground forces; and General Simic, I believe. This is another change that came about at a later point, not in December as most of the changes that took place. This was done sometimes -- this was done sometime in April, late March or early April possibly. This is another usual document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You had a chance to inspect individual files, personnel files, in relation to persons who were appointed between December and these last changes that were introduced in April 1999. Were there any appointments -- were any candidates appointed who failed to meet the criteria? Were there any significant discrepancies in terms of the candidates' experience, previous command functions, I mean between those who were being replaced and those who were being appointed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: As for all these new appointments, each appointee met all the criteria that were required for his respective post. All the newly appointed officers who were now being appointed -- or at least 99 per cent of them enjoyed certain comparative advantages in relation to those who preceded them in terms of experience, in terms of the different posts that they had previously held, in terms of their success rates, in terms of their level of training and military background. There is not the slightest doubt about this. I even have documents showing this, copies of their records which can be cross-referenced. There is no doubt about this whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, my last question: The Prosecutor has a theory in this trial which goes as follows: Once General Ojdanic had been appointed Chief of the General Staff, many changes were made to the officers' ranks in the VJ. Certain people were eliminated who opposed the use of the VJ in Kosovo. General, I should assume that you at least attended certain meetings at which these personnel changes were discussed. In your opinion, was this actually an element that was considered when the personnel changes were made that you, yourself, witnessed between December 1998 and March 1999?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I rise to object to foundation on this question is based upon. He's asking for an opinion. Now, I agree in certain circumstances one can give an opinion, but the previous statement that counsel made is about an assumption which he, counsel, makes, which he asks him to make to express an opinion on the basis of that assumption. I think perhaps a proper foundation could be laid or the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What would be wrong with the question: As far as you could tell was any of this done to eliminate opposition to the use of the VJ in Kosovo? Which is the same question in different language. Is there anything wrong with that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question as put there is, on the face of it, an unobjectionable question; but to ask the question in the form that I see to be asked by counsel here, which is asking the witness to assume what counsel knows or believes is an improper way to go about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you prepared to rephrase your question, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in a way, you took part in these personnel changes, you were present, I assume, at least at part of these meetings where these personnel changes were being discussed; am I right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Was it pointed out at any time that these personnel changes were taking place because some of the persons who were being replaced opposed the use of the army in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Not in that form.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it had been a question of disobedience, as stated here, in that case other measures would be taken vis-a-vis these officers or generals, rather. They wouldn't have been given any new appointments, they would have been dismissed from their duties and other legal measures would have been taken if that had been the case. That's not the kind of discussion that took place with regard to these officers. The new Chief of General Staff exercised his right to choose the people he would work with in the future; that is his right. So this kind of qualification was not stated, at least not when I was present, and when the material was being prepared for the session of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, it's probably because it's so early in the morning, but can you remind me of the meaning of the letters VSO, is that Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We have a couple of questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. General, I have just a few questions for you. In paragraph 5 of your statement you say, or rather, you refer to the powers of the president of the FRY for appointments, dismissals, personnel changes, establishment positions for generals, and so on, and you say this falls exclusively within the authority of the president as regulated by Article 136 of the constitution and 151 of the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me Article 5.4, you explained the procedure, you explained the procedure, how the -- how proposals were made to the military cabinet of the president of the FRY, and after sessions of the Supreme Defence Council a conclusion would be sent back to you -- to the General Staff, rather. Could you just explain to me in which form of document this conclusion was submitted to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: After a session was held of the Supreme Defence Council, to give one example, most often what was on the agenda were other issues as well. I as the person who was supposed to prepare the realisation of the adopted conclusions and adopted decisions, I received only an excerpt of the minutes pertaining to personnel matters; that is to say that this document was a list where the secretary of the Supreme Defence Council confirms with his signature that he transmitted to me the tasks that were to be carried out by way of implementing the conclusions of the Supreme Defence Council. So it is not a decision, it is simply an excerpt from the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: General, on the basis of these minutes you prepare that formal part of the decision, or rather, the president's decree itself. And then you submit this decree for signature, or rather, you submit it to the --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- So that the president would sign this decree on appointment, dismissal, et cetera, of a particular person as for this particular post?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In this very same paragraph you say that this decree means the materialisation of the decision of the Supreme Defence Council. Could you please explain to me what you meant -- just wait for a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honour, we have the very same -- I used the word "ukaz", and I believe we spent a lot of time explaining it should be -- it is quite different from decree, which is "uredba", and I know that the interpreters are accustom to using the decree, but I would really insist that some other word is used, whether it is ordinance or -- because the distinction in our opinion is very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the English translation of the statement, 3D1118, the language used is "a document (order)" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. If we are talking on -- that's a very -- that's paragraph 4 of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 5.4 of his -- last sentence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the Serbian it says: "Which prepares the act (ukaz)" ordinance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you say that's different from an order, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh yes, very much different, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the -- I believe the Professor Markovic explained the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What did he say, remind us?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the difference between the decree -- the difference which I had in mind is between the decree and the ordinance. The decree is a specific act which is done by -- only by the government; an ordinance, "ukaz," is a specific document which is only according to our legal system and constitutional system, in the hands of the president. So the president is the only person who can issue an ordinance. There is no other body in the system that can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that distinction the same as the distinction between making legislation and promulgating legislation or is that a different distinction?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it's a different distinction. I wouldn't be able to answer your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- Your question now. But in a sense of promulgating the legislation is done by the very same kind of document, which is "ukaz."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your point is adequately made now in the transcript, Mr. Zecevic, and you've got the Serbian into the English translation as well and you will have a chance to make submissions in due course. If there's anything else on the factual situation you need to ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. Thank you very much. I just have one or two more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, this procedure that you explained in paragraph 5 pertains to the time before the state of war was declared, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: General, during the state of war appointments were also made at this level of establishment, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In which form, or rather, let me ask you this way. Do you know whether sessions of the Supreme Defence Council were held during the course of the war and did you get such excerpts from the conclusions, or rather, excerpts from the minutes containing conclusions on appointments of specific individuals to specific positions?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: During the war period, the entire composition, or rather, a particular part of the composition of the General Staff, rather, officers comprising the collegium of the General Staff were the command post where the supreme commander was, or rather, the president. I did not attend these meetings. I was not at that location ever. As for personnel changes, as for changes that took place during the course of the war, during the war period, discussions were held at the Supreme Command. In terms of all the authority that was there with regard to this personnel, it was the president who had that authority. And I as a technical organ only spelled this out into a current document by way of realisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you, if I understood you well, you would get an order on the appointment of a particular individual to a particular post during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you do not know whether a session was held of the Supreme Defence Council after the 23rd of March, 1999, I mean I'm talking about the war period of 78 days?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Since I got tasks from this area, I never -- well, I could not conclude that a meeting had been held of the Supreme Defence Council, but practically of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I take you back -- can I take you back to the question Mr. Zecevic asked there at the beginning of this chapter. He asked if during the war you ever received excerpts from minutes containing conclusions on appointments of specific individuals to specific positions. Could you answer that yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just the last question. General, the procedure of using abbreviations in the Army of Yugoslavia, is it prescribed in a document of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Abbreviations that are used in the army are regulated through instructions, if I remember correctly now, on conducting a working file and all the abbreviations are listed there and how they should be used. That is the instructions on the work of staffs and the use of work maps. I think that that is what it is called.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing. VK, that's an abbreviation that denotes the supreme commander, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: VK-DA, is that the Supreme Command, "Vrhovna Komanda"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Stamp on behalf of the Prosecution. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is the peacetime complement of generals and admirals in the VJ before the war in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: If I understood your question correctly, generals and admirals in the army were at the highest positions, high command positions or top positions in the Army of Yugoslavia; that is to say duties which according to establishment require the rank of general or admiral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know what Mr. Stamp asked. I see that part of his words are missing here in the transcript and the interpretation the witness received is a bit illogical. I mean, it's all the same to me if Mr. Stamp is happy with this answer, but I'm not sure if that was the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question actually is complete in the English transcript, but it obviously has been translated differently because it wasn't that question that was answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General, how many generals and admirals were there in the VJ shortly before the war started in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: I do not recall the exact figure. It is around 70, the total number of admirals and generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the appointments during peacetime were made by the president in consultation with the SDC; is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: The president, only in accordance with the constitution of -- and the Law on the Army, he is the only one in charge of admirals and generals, but in his decisions he can consult the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in making appointments he would have before him a number of individuals' names from which he could choose; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Is it correct that he would have before him, prepared by your directorate, by your group, a number of names of individuals from which he and those who advised him on the Supreme Defence Council selected the person to be appointed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Stamp, I would like to intervene here to request you to tell me what you mean by appointments, is it transfers or is it promotions? Because that is a bit of a confusing part of the word. It can be used either way. What do you mean by that, first of all, kindly?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I should say appointment to a post, an establishment post, that a general or an admiral should occupy. The president would have before him a list of names from which he would make -- he and the Supreme Defence Council make a selection; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: As for the complement was concerned and as far as any kind of personnel changes in terms of admirals and generals were concerned, he would receive a proposal from the General Staff, where the General Staff would be proposing such and such a change, and it is the president who makes the final decision as to whether he accepts the proposal or not. After that, that decision is carried through.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Fezer, you're not focusing on what I want to know. I want to know if when he had to make the decision and when the Supreme Defence Council met in making these decisions, if they had before them a list of names of individuals that were proposed for any establishment post?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And they would make their selection from that list?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: But -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, what we're primarily concerned about here is dismissal from posts, removal from posts. You were asked -- I note -- I noted that you said that you were in charge of a technical body and you don't know the reasons for the changes; however, you were asked by counsel to give your opinion about what you heard and what you understood to be the reasons for changes. So can I ask you about a few of them, and I want to focus on the removal from office because that is what the main allegation in this case is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I'm sorry to intervene again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: These are technical words, dismissal is a technical word, removal is a technical word, transfer is a technical word.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: So I think you will kindly be more specific on this because it will lead to a lot of confusion. These are very technical words in the services.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's speak about the removal of the commander of the 2nd Army in April and his replacement to General Grahovac -- sorry, with General Obradovic. Do you recall that, that that occurred?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Not exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look at P721, please -- sorry, it's 3D721.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is -- these are the minutes of a meeting of the Supreme Command, and we have Major -- I'm sorry, I'm afraid I have the wrong document before me. Sorry, it is the correct document, I have the wrong page reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we just go to page 5 of the English, and this is page 4 in the B/C/S copy, top of page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You will see an item 4 there, and this is the Chief of General Staff speaking and he is saying that: "There must be no talk about the replacement of the commander of the 2nd Army." This is dated the 3rd --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: I see it. Well, this document -- well, I'm not aware of this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: -- I did not attend -- this is a meeting of the Supreme Command, I was not there, so -- well, I've never seen this kind of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did you know that the commander of the 2nd Army, and I ask you again now, was replaced in early April 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: I said at the beginning that those were not dismissals -- or at least that's not how those personnel changes were described --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm asking you now --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: -- The word "dismissal" was used in those cases where certain persons failed to meet certain criteria or they failed to carry out their tasks, so they were as a result dismissed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question is: Did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the problem we're looking at is here appears to be a change in personnel that you don't know about; that's the point that Mr. Stamp seems to be making. That could happen, could it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I knew about changes only insofar as I prepared certain documents, but I never learned the reasons, nor were these reasons ever explained to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you knew about this change, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I drafted the document which enshrined this change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, was there an element of secrecy involved in this change, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: No. There could have been no secrecy. It was carried through and it was public.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When it became public, wasn't it a matter of public debate and public concern in Montenegro, where the 2nd Army was based; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's look at P1352. This is a document on the list of exhibits that was put up by learned counsel for Mr. Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document says in the middle there -- it's a news report, I should tell you, of the 4th of February, and it says: "The pro-Milosevic SMP (Socialist People's Party) in Montenegro sent official word, through its paper, 'Dan,' that its relationship with the VJ were better than those of any other part, and that as a result the VJ itself was more inclined towards it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to raise our usual objection when documents like these are used. I don't think Mr. Stamp can ask the witness anything based on this document, since -- we can only raise all the usual objections that we have been raising in relation to media articles being a translation of a document that had already been translated. So the translation of a translation, plus it contains additional comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fezer, I wonder if you could just briefly leave the courtroom with the usher until we deal with this objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, that's not an accurate statement of the position. We will not use documents of this nature as establishing the truth of their contents, and one of the reasons is one that you've given about translation. But if Mr. Stamp, by using it, gets answers from the witness whereby he agrees with comments in this article, then the position is completely different. So that's been our policy all along. There's no reason why he can't pose the question this way. If he gets a denial of any acceptance of this, then this is of no value; but if the witness accepts it, then the position is quite different, he's confirming the accuracy of it, it makes it authentic because he's got personal knowledge. So let's have the witness back and ask him to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while he's coming back I should add that this document is on the list of counsel for Mr. Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not even certain that I have this document in my list, by the way. [In English] I'm sorry, I will check my list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fezer, listen again to the question and do your best to answer it. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I was just referring you to a news report, and I'm going to ask you a question shortly. The report continues: "The new commander of the 2nd Army is Lieutenant-Colonel-General Milorad Obradovic and Major-General Jago Stevanovic has been appointed Chief of Staff of this army. Radosav Martinovic has been appointed an advisor in the Federal Defence Ministry which cannot be interpreted other than as a demotion within the VJ." So first question is this: Wasn't the appointment of Milorad Obradovic to be the head of the 2nd Army viewed by many persons in military circles as the appointment of a Milosevic loyalist to a position of control in the course of the war? From the meetings you attended, was it resisted, the appointment resisted, on that basis?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: I didn't attend this specific meeting and I can't comment, nor can I provide my own opinion. Decisions were for the president to take, and it wasn't highly surprising that General Obradovic should be appointed commander of the 2nd Army. I don't see any reason for that to cause any other kinds of different. I don't see for that to cause any other comments --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You say --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It appears to be -- now it's corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Wasn't it a fact, though, that senior person in the army were removed and appointed to -- or offered appointments to positions as advisors in the federal government? And these appointments were generally regarded as demotions?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Is there a question? I don't think there can be any talk of demotion because --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: -- All those who were transferred from their duties to political bodies had all the same elements that attached to their previous appointment --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on then. Did it --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. I'm not sure the witness was permitted to fully answer the question. I think he was interrupted in the middle of his answer, and he should be entitled to answer it I would think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, he did answer. He was going on to say -- to add to his answer, which can be explored in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's answered the question, Mr. Ackerman. I appreciate that he had not completed what he intended to say, and if that -- if Mr. Visnjic wants to follow that up, he's free to do so in due course. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you aware that General Perisic was removed in a manner that was illegal or inappropriate?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Illegal it wasn't. As for the manner being appropriate or not, I don't think there's any point in talking about that because the same procedure was applied that was invariably applied every time someone changed position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the meetings that you attended and in the discussions that you had, did you become aware that General Perisic said that his removal was done in a manner which was illegal and inappropriate?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look at P935 and I believe, happily, I have the right page. Could we go to page 27 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You can see the cover of that document, it is the minutes of the collegium meeting of the General Staff of the 11th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Page 27 in English is page 25 in B/C/S. I'm sorry I should have pointed that out earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I won't read it all to you, but General Risto Matkovic is making a presentation for the discussions about what to do with General Perisic; his situation had to be resolved. And he referred to the decree of the president of the 24th of November, whereby General Perisic was appointed an advisor to the federal government. And that General Perisic held official talks with Federal Prime Minister Momir Bulatovic and said he appreciated the offer but would not accept it, and handed over his duties as Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army on the 27th of November, 1998, and I will get to a part which I would like to read into the record: "On the 27th of November, 1998, General Perisic made and signed a statement for the public of the following contents. The current regime does not like leaders of high integrity and those who use their own heads to think. I was removed from the position of Chief of General Staff of the Yugoslav Army without consultations in an inappropriate and illegal manner. I do not accept the invented position in the current federal government that has been offered to me. I remain at the disposal of my army -- I remain at the disposal to my army, state, and people." I'll ask you again, weren't you aware, sir, as a person in charge of the directorate for the cadre of generals of the public controversy surrounding the removal of General Perisic in which he claimed it was done in an inappropriate and illegal fashion? Weren't you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: I must say again that all these things that happened were not things that I knew about. I was part of a technical body in the General Staff. I would merely transform certain decisions and conclusions into appropriate documents; therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But before we get into that, I'm asking you about one thing. It's respect to an answer you gave to me earlier that you didn't hear about it that he was complaining about the way he was removed. And the question is simply this: Did you not become aware of the controversy surrounding the removal of General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Because he was directly in touch with the highest level, the president specifically; he never talked to the lower levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. That is your answer.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, based on the meetings you attended and in your capacity as chief of the department that dealt with the cadre of generals, that General Dimitrijevic claimed that illegal activities were being carried out with the aim of replacing him and appointing a new chief of the VJ security department? Did you in your capacity or in any capacity become aware of that claim?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: This was before the beginning of the aggression against the FRY. As for any talks that he held, this is not something that I know anything about; but same as before, I was tasked with preparing a document appointing General Dimitrijevic to the federal defence ministry, the position being advisor to the defence minister on security matters. That is all I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You are aware, sir, that he refused to accept that post or to take up that post as well?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: He did not like this, but he accepted this and he eventually took up his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When did he take up that position, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Just after this state was regulated, after the ordinance was adopted; I'm not sure when.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. We'll get back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at P932.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to comment on something which General Dimitrijevic said, and if you could briefly look at the cover page to identify what it is. You'll see, sir, that it is the collegium minutes of the 4th of February, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it's page 7 in English, which is the top of page 6 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I'll just read it. This is General Dimitrijevic addressing General Ojdanic in this collegium meeting. "For these reasons, as my room for work has been quite limited lately and certain illegal activities, so to speak, are carried out with the aim of replacing me and appointing a new chief of administration - and, unfortunately, you too are either taking part in it or your name is being manipulated - I am asking that an interview with the president of the SRJ be scheduled for me." You never, sir, became aware in your capacity of these controversies or this controversy of surrounding the removal of General Dimitrijevic, that he was claiming that there were illegal activities being conducted in order to remove him? Is it your evidence that you never knew about these things?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. And you know what Generals Perisic and Dimitrijevic were speaking of when they said "illegal activities"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: I don't know what activities these would be, but the procedure and the way the document was adopted was perfectly legal in each of these cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fezer, over what period were you the person in charge of drafting the ordinances that gave effect to these changes in the positions held by members of the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, throughout this period --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When did it start? When did you first take up that particular responsibility, was it in 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Earlier on, a lot earlier, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How often were you involved in an ordinance which transferred a senior member of the VJ to become an advisor in the Federal Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every time there was an ordinance like that throughout that period, General Perisic, General Dimitrijevic, and General Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All these documents -- no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm interested to know if there were any more such appointments.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not apart from these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is an advisor in the Federal Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the duties of an advisor are set out in the rules governing the work of the relevant ministry; therefore, I'd be ill-advised trying to answer this question specifically, but I know what his job was in the army and I can only assume that his job would have been somewhat similar, the new one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I know you've said that these people would still enjoy the same trappings of office as they had in the VJ, but an advisor sounds like somebody who doesn't have direct command responsibilities, and therefore might not be seen to be in such a prestigious position as when he was a general before with executive responsibilities. Is that a fair way of looking at it or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could agree with that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: So therefore, the Ministry of Defence -- in the Ministry of Defence when they were appointed as advisor, this was like a dumping-ground, isn't it, for these generals to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Yes, because obviously when they would be taken away from the cadre position into an ex-cadre position like with the federal government and they were appointed as advisors, well that is like taking away people and dumping them into the Ministry of Defence. Was that the position or were they really performing something very active there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were performing their functions. It would definitely -- would be a bit too rough of a formulation to say that the defence ministry was some sort of a dumping-ground on to which these persons were tipped. I don't think I could accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before I move on, just to follow-up on that. What rank were you in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you know, sir, that there were occasions when the president or the SDC disregarded proposals of the Chief of General Staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Not throughout this period, but the answer would be: Yes, in relation to a period a lot earlier on. This was known to happen, that a proposal of the General Staff was not accepted and that the president's decision was actually different from the proposal itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, let's focus on the period from mid-1998 to -- through to mid-1999. Do you know of situations where the proposals of the Chief of General Staff were disregarded by the SDC or by the president?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know of assignments or promotions to positions established for generals being made without any consultation with the Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We were looking at the minutes of the collegium session of 4th of February, 1999, that's P932.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to look at another page, another part of that record, that's page 12 in English, and which is page 10, the last paragraph of page 10 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I'd like to read that. General Ojdanic is here saying -- or maybe I should start from the top to put everything in context. General Dimitrijevic asks: "Doesn't the law say that generals are appointed and promoted at the proposal of the Chief of General Staff?" General Ojdanic says: "I believe, Aca, that it is much clearer to you than to me both in the preceding and the current period." To which General Dimitrijevic replies:" All right. I need to know what to ask in the other place. So the law does not apply." So which General Ojdanic says: "This is only a proposal, and it is up to the president, and it is his constitutional right, but the proposals are also not only disregarded ... No proposal needs to be made at all, and the president of the FRY -- of the SRJ will decide as he sees fit."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That position which General Ojdanic takes at that meeting, is that surprising to you then?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you -- therefore you are aware that at that period proposals of the Chief of General Staff are not only disregarded sometimes, but sometimes no need to be made at all for the president to decide if he sees fit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I doubt if your first statement is an accurate one based on this alone, Mr. Stamp. All this is saying that the president's entitled to do as he sees fit, but there is no statement there that that has actually happened without consultation, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The general says: "Proposals are also not only disregarded. No proposal needs to be made at all." And they are speaking in the context of a question asked by General Dimitrijevic whether or not generals are appointed and promoted at the proposal of the Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In most cases, yes. The proposal of the General Staff was always there when decisions were made on appointments or any other kind of regulating the situation in the service, but it is the constitutional right for the president to decide as he sees best.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I agree with that, but -- let me ask you this simply then: Do you agree with the statement of General Ojdanic made on that date that proposals of the Chief of General Staff are also not only disregarded, do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: I think that here General Ojdanic said that it is possible that something like that could happen in practice, but he did not take an example and he did not confirm that any one of his proposals had not been accepted. This is a possibility that he mentions as the president's constitutional right, and that is what he says to General Dimitrijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you agree with his statement that in respect to exercising his right to appoint and promote generals, the president, President Milosevic, needed to have no proposals before him at all? You will agree with that as well?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It is possible -- or as a matter of fact, it is regulated by the constitution that it is his right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on quickly to P1298.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Incidentally, do you know about the removal from office of General Grahovac during the war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: To the extent to which I know about all others. I just got the task to prepare an appropriate document that the decision would -- the president would have to sign, but I would not be familiar with how the decision was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know of public controversy against surrounding his dismissal and removal -- well, his removal from his position?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Well, I do remember probably -- well, there were media that wrote about that, but it's nothing specific that I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was he made an advisor in the federal ministry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I have to ask one question. Somebody used the word that the position in the Ministry of Defence were invented. It means there weren't vacancies in the Ministry of Defence for generals, and they were being sent against vacancies which were being created, is it? Or were there existing vacancies to which they were transferred? Do you know the situation, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There weren't any such positions in the organization of the ministry, but the president, according to the constitution, could set positions in the state where generals would be appointed. So by virtue of passing the ordinance, he prescribed the position in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And this position did not exist in the ministry already, that's what you're saying? I mean, this was created, these positions were created in the ministry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's being pointed out to me that, in fact, Grahovac may have been appointed an advisor to the president of -- defence advisor to the president of Montenegro rather than to the federal ministry. Do you recollect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, slip of the tongue. I know he was removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. If it's convenient to the Court, I would have just five minute left, but perhaps we could take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, I'm happy if you've got five minutes, we'll continue for these five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I ask you do you recall whether General Grahovac was appointed as an advisor to the -- an advisor in the federal government for Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what we've just been dealing with. He was appointed an advisor to the president of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I'm wondering if he would help us with whether or not he later became an advisor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not that's correct, he became an advisor in the federal government or appointed an advisor in the federal government and later on became an advisor to the president of Montenegro, do you know that? If you do not, you could just say so.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: By the decision made then, he was appointed advisor in the Government of Montenegro, and he remained at that position until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know of him making public statements to the effect ...

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Well, yes, there were things like that in the newspapers, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In fact, he said that there was a purge of people like himself, General Perisic, General Dimitrijevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: It is possible that he used that particular expression, but this is, quite simply, a reaction of a man who perhaps was not satisfied with his status and so on and so forth --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: So he was kind of passionate about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And he like the others were saying that it was because they were not loyal to President Milosevic; do you recall that being the matter or the issue of controversy?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: I don't know. It is their relationships. That, quite simply, was not accessible to me, except for what could sort of be heard on the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I don't think I have anything further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Your Honour, but I think it's perhaps better for us to take the break now because I need to reorganize things as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fezer, we need to have a break at this stage for 20 minutes. Please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we'll see you at 25 minutes past 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fezer, a few more questions from Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please see 3D721, page 5 in the English text and page 4 in B/C/S. 3D721. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you remember when Mr. Stamp asked you about this exhibit, and this is the briefing of the 3rd of April, 1999, and when he drew your attention to paragraph 4 in General Ojdanic's remarks, when General Ojdanic says that there should be no talk about the replacement of the commander of the 2nd Army. And then Mr. Stamp suggested to you that this had to do with a big secret, that there was secrecy involved, as he said. Could you please look at the first page of this document in both versions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in around the middle of the page in English. We're just waiting for the first page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, before you is General Branko Krga's statement. I would like to draw your attention to -- well, it's around the middle of the page in B/C/S as well, to what he says. "In the west there are speculations about the change of commander of the -- of the 2nd Army. I propose a statement be issued about that." General, I know that you said that you were not present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But let me ask you, when you look at what General Krga said and what General Ojdanic said, do you see any big secret involved, or rather, that the replacement of the commander of the 2nd Army was carried out secretly, without people knowing about it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: In my view, there is no secrecy involved here, particularly even if one wanted to conceal that, people would find out and people did know about it. It could be seen in the media, in the public, so it could not have been a big secret on any account.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility that what General Ojdanic stated has to do with General Krga's proposals, that an -- that the army issue a press release in view of the replacement of General Martinovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1352, please, could we have that displayed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It's the news article that Mr. Stamp showed you, and he also suggested to you that it was some kind of political replacement, the replacement of General Martinovic. I would like to ask you to read the last paragraph of this news article.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Towards the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, towards the bottom.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Should I read it out loud?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. "Those knowledgeable about events."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: "Those knowledgeable about events in Montenegro and Yugoslavia say that in his career today General Obradovic displayed no clear signs of a readiness to see the army involved in the resolution of political disputes, rather, he sticks to the army's professional character."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, as far as you know General Obradovic, does he look like a yes-man to you, someone who blindly obeyed President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: To the extent to which I can make an assessment, I think that General Obradovic is a highly disciplined officer, a high-ranking general, and as for the views he held he defended them and he fought for his views. So I could not consider him to be a yes-man, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now have a look at the next exhibit Mr. Stamp showed you, that is P935, page 29 in B/C/S, page 31 in English. General, before we see it on our monitors, you remember that Mr. Stamp also suggested to you how General Perisic was replaced and let's see what the collegium had to say about that at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the third paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, please bear in mind that in re-examination it's not proper to pose leading questions. Now, this may not be a leading question, but it sounds as though it might be. And the value is nil if -- in re-examination if matters are dealt with by leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's not going to be a leading question. I just want to point out some parts of the text. It is totally irrelevant what the witness's comment to all of this is going to be. I just want the witness to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In that case there's no need to put it to the witness. You can point it out to us in your submissions in due course. The only point of putting any of this to the witness is to get his answer, if he's got one that can be of assistance to the Trial Chamber. But you don't need to go through an argumentation exercise at this stage -- in fact, it's wrong to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the end I would like the witness to confirm something for us about a fact that is not in -- is not related to what Mr. Stamp had put to him, that is what I wanted to say. So in order to do that, I have to go through this text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a matter for you how you conduct it, but if you're going to show him a fact and then ask him about it, that sounds like a leading question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if I could -- if it's not related to anything I put before him, now I have concerns about whether it's appropriate for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Is it something arising out of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, it is arising from cross-examination, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So please, paragraph 3, General Dimitrijevic's remarks. General, do you know that General Perisic sent a request to the General Staff, asking to have his status resolved?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: He submitted a request after the ordinance on his removal was passed and he was transferred to the federal government. He was not satisfied with that decision and he wanted to have his status resolved in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. And over here in paragraph 3 of General Dimitrijevic's remarks, or rather, what was it that General Dimitrijevic proposed? How should the status be resolved?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Well, General Dimitrijevic proposed to have a talk with General Perisic, and it only could have been the president or someone appointed by the president. And then in this kind of talk, a decision would be made how to proceed further, of course if he were not to accept the position that he had been proposed for.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at the same document, page 30 in the B/C/S, 32 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you see General Ojdanic's contribution down that page? The 11th of March, 1999, General Ojdanic says: "We do not need any new scandals and I will not make any further comments. I have my own view ... overall behaviour and overall action ... but we really... the path covered by General Perisic and the overall situation in the army and in the country ... it would be inappropriate ... possibly counter-productive in any way, but of course we know that this is within the competence of the president of the FRY and he will take this decision." General, my question about this: Do you know what the final decision was, how the issue of General Perisic was eventually resolved following this request by General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Since it was accepted and it was impossible to reinstall him in the ranks of the army which he requested, he was offered a position to him in the federal government. A document was passed terminating his service, and that was the final touch to this issue, if I may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So General Ojdanic's contribution is a result of what exactly the discussion that preceded this at a collegium meeting or what?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Yes, there was a discussion about this at a collegium meeting, this was the conclusion, and the conclusion was submitted to the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let me ask you about the following officers. Do you know General Simic spent some time in the defence ministry?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when he left and what became of him later, did he ever return?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: I don't remember the date he left, but he took up a post in the ministry, after which he was back in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What about General Velickovic, did he follow a similar path?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: He was deputy defence minister, after which he was returned and appointed assistant Chief of the General Staff for the air force and anti-air defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What about General Farkas, was he too first in the VJ and then in the defence ministry and then back in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Previously Farkas had been outside the army. He was a regional secretary for All People's Defence in Vojvodina, he also worked for the ministry for a while, after which he was appointed chief of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And now something in relation to General Grahovac. You said that General Grahovac ended up as an advisor in Montenegro's government or an advisor to the president of Montenegro, I'm not certain?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, this position that he held in Montenegro's government, was this a position with no influence whatsoever? Did he have any influence over the work of Montenegro's government, can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO FEZER
utterances.text: I can't tell you in any great detail what his responsibilities were in the government, but I can tell you what the ordinance stated. He became advisor of the president for defence issues. He retired from that post, so all of this was outside the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fezer, that completes your evidence; thank you for coming here to give it. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next week is Stanisa Ivkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another 92 ter witness. The statement is 3D117.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you mean 3D1117?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1117, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ivkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document now being shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You'll now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, on the 20th of August, 2007, did you make a statement to the Ojdanic Defence team, which you subsequently signed?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Upon your arrival in The Hague, did you look at that statement?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You say you have several amendments to make to this statement. Can we please take this one step at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Defence Exhibit 3D1117, can that be displayed, page 4 in the B/C/S, page 4 in the English, paragraph 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, what were your amendments to this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: It was only about this abbreviation, OC. It read OV originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as I remember, there's the second-last line, OC, again did you have any remarks to make about that?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How should it read instead?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right. It reads: "So they were not all accessible to OC personnel or to him."

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: It says "or to him," and it should read "or to me."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right. What about the next line?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Again, the same thing "to me," as opposed to "to him" or "himself."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page in the B/C/S, please, paragraph 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You had an amendment to make to the first line of that paragraph, didn't you. Can you tell us what it's about?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. It's about the word "provisions," the word "provisions," "orders that I was informed about did not contain provisions." Instead of "provisions," it should read "information."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next, paragraph 26, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First line of paragraph 26, it reads: "ODI," it should be "DOI." This is the official abbreviation for the so-called daily operations report, that's the first line and the same applies to line 3 in English. Instead of "ODI" it should read "DOI."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, so much for the amendments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions, Colonel. You provided a very detailed account in your statement of the functioning and work of the operations centre. At the beginning of the war, before the beginning of the war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. You should ask the formal questions, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Mr. Visnjic, in case we omit that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, having made these amendments, were you to testify before this Court would you provide all the same answers to all the same questions as reflected in your statement, 3D1117?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the beginning of the war, where was the operations centre of the General Staff of the VJ physically located?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't hear the interpreters interpreting, therefore I'm not sure when I'm supposed to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You just go ahead and I'll tell you if there are any problems.

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: The operations centre was at building A of the General Staff of the VJ. There was a special facility that was meant to be used for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The 24th, that was when NATO attacked Yugoslavia. Were there any changes in the work of the General Staff? Were there any changes in the work of the operations centre?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were changes. The VJ was put at full combat-readiness, and this applied to the operations centre because it was part of the army; it too was placed at full combat-readiness. This implies an increase in the numbers and quality of the operations duty team, which was working 24-hour shifts, around-the-clock, at the operations centre.
