The operations centre was working all year round, 365 days a year, and this same principle applied during NATO's aggression against our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did the General Staff at one point in time move to a different location; if so, when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Part of the General Staff, including its chief, left for the basic command post as soon as on the 24th. The remaining part of the General Staff stayed on until the 4th of April, if I'm not mistaken, because threats had been made that the General Staff would be one of the targets. Due to these threats, the remaining part of the General Staff left this peacetime location as well, and they also moved to wartime command posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, the operations centre remained for another ten days or so?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. The operations centre remained in that installation all of the ten days and worked. If I may, one digression, on both command posts -- that is, to both command posts I sent one or two persons to prepare the ground for admitting the operations centre as a whole, if need be, but the operations centre was there the whole time, until they left the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now, in those ten days, how did the information, the data that remained at the General Staff and that the operations centre processed there, how was it submitted to the Chief of the General Staff and the other part of the General Staff that was at the command post?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Since combat activities had already started, the subordinate commands and units sent to the General Staff daily, regular and interim and combat reports. The team on duty at the General Staff processed this information, wrote up a comprehensive report on the situation in the army, and by 6.00 in the morning that report was submitted to the group that was already at the command post headed by the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And how long did that go on?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Until the 4th, if I remember correctly the date of departure from the peacetime location.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What about later, after the 4th?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: After the 4th, the operations centre fully took up position at its basic wartime location, at the basic and rear command posts. In view of the existing technical possibilities and work organization, the centre was outside the operations room is so that it did not -- not regularly receive those written daily and operations reports any longer; it was done instead by a special communications centre. And reports were submitted directly to the operations team on duty at the command post. So the personnel of the operations centre no longer had any direct contact with the reports of the subordinate units and commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well, daily reports of subordinate units arrived at the communications centre?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Via the communications centre they arrived directly to the operations team on duty at the command post where the technical bodies of the General Staff processed them, and on that basis a comprehensive daily operations report was written up for the army. And it was forwarded to users according to the instructions for the work of the operations team. This was done by the operations administration, and all organizational units of the General Staff were involved in writing the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I are no further questions for this witness. He gave a detailed statement, so my questioning is here complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm receiving some written communications from my client that I'm having difficulty dealing with. I may have questions for this witness, but I think I would need to have a break to consult with my client before I could make that determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How long will this take, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No more than ten minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivkovic, we'll need to break for ten minutes just now. Please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we'll see you back here at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Break taken at 11.05 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do have some questions and I deeply appreciate the opportunity to consult with my client. I thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'd like you to look at a document, it's -- exhibit number is 4D275, and the part of that -- this is a combat report from the 3rd Army to the General Staff and it's dated the 2nd of April, 1999. And what I'm interested in is the first paragraph right above paragraph 3.2 which is on page 2 in English and probably the same page in B/C/S. Now, in paragraph 11 of your statement you told us: "The reports of the commands of the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps, the regular ones, and interim as needed enabled the General Staff to be informed of events in Kosovo and Metohija and the activities of the commands and units, that on the basis of this information the General Staff took appropriate measures to stabilise the situation, protect the endangered population, increase the protection of the state border, and features of special importance, protection of transport convoys, and the like." And then with regard to those reports in paragraph 13 you said: "They make no mention of organized crimes, but only of possible individual cases against which appropriate legal measures were promptly taken in order to prevent," it says "this occurrence," but probably the translation should be "reoccurrence." Now, this document you have in front of you right above paragraph 3.2 there's a paragraph which reports on the military prosecutor's receipt of criminal complaints, the filing of 17 investigation requests, and the issuance of five indictments, that there were 15 on-site investigations, 9 individuals detained, 72 investigation requests, five individuals charged. 78 of those related to failure to respond to mobilisation and avoiding military service, while the rest refer to other criminal offences. Now, I take it that's the kind of report you were referring to in paragraph 13 where you talked about individual cases that were reported by these daily combat reports from the 3rd Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It was stated there that these were only individual cases, those that were treated, because there weren't any cases en masse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And there was a report, I take it a daily report, that went from the General Staff to the supreme commander based upon the reports received from the various units; is that true?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you know if that report was basically a process of cutting and pasting, where everything, for instance, that General Pavkovic would report was sent to the supreme commander or was it a selective process where only certain things were included in the report to the supreme commander?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot assert that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you see those reports that went to the supreme commander?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Only those at the time when I was in the operations duty team doing my shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And during that time, did you notice that General Pavkovic's reports regarding the activities of the courts and the prosecutor's offices were rather routinely omitted from the report to the supreme commander; did you notice that?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: That was not in my line of work; therefore, I could not have observed any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, this document that you have in front of you, would you say -- would you agree that that was fairly typical of the kind of reports contained in the daily combat reports coming up from General Pavkovic regarding the activities of the courts and the Prosecutor's offices in the 3rd Army area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: I repeat, the judiciary part was not in my line of work and I did not take care of that. That was supposed to be done by other organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think there was a translation problem or something. I don't think you -- I think you misunderstood. This report you're looking at, do you know that there are a number of reports on a daily basis from the 3rd Army that contain a paragraph similar to this, reporting activity with regard to crimes? You've seen those and you know that they exist, don't you?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw the reports. It is possible that -- well, I admit, it's been eight years, I don't recall the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall if this was a typical part of those combat reports, to report on activities of the prosecutor's office and the judicial organs?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot assert that that is typical, but there were such cases -- such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you know of any instance- and you may not have even had an opportunity to know - but do you know of any instance where General Pavkovic was asked by the General Staff or the supreme commander to provide more detailed information regarding any of these reports about the activity of the prosecutor's office and the judicial organs?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: I repeat, I was not at the command post all the time, but only at the time when I was doing my shift. I had other tasks, too. Therefore, I can say even less, that this is typical. I'm saying that organs of the legal department, or rather, judiciary organs were involved in this, organs that are in charge of this, whose line of work this is. Quite simply, this was not the work of the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe I'm misunderstanding. Are you saying that the judiciary and the prosecutor's offices had a separate duty to report to the General Staff on their activities, in addition to these reports from General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot assert that because I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. The question I asked you before again I think was misunderstood. Are you aware of any request from the General Staff to General Pavkovic to provide additional information regarding his reports about the activities of the prosecutor's office, for instance.

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot assert that either. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That's all I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. You will now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir, since we are looking at this document, 4D275, can we go back to the part that you were shown, I think it's page 2 of the English, and I don't know if that corresponds to the B/C/S, but we are talking about the part of this report that begins at 3, so it would be the next page in B/C/S, page 2 in English. Page 2 in B/C/S. The part that you were referred to just now about complaints being filed, can you see that it falls under the general heading of army manpower levels according to wartime establishment? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Firstly deals with the amount of officers, non-commissioned officers, privates, volunteers, and then it deals with complaints in that context, which is what you were referred to, and it points out that there were -- of all the investigation requests received 78 are relating to criminal offences of failing to respond to mobilisation -- to a mobilisation call and avoiding military service. You see that?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And below that it goes on to talk about losses in personnel and it gives figures for that as well, correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page in English, that's page 3 in English, and it's the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see a paragraph, 5, there deals with security in the army, separate and distinct rubric from manpower issues.

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Covered within two paragraphs, two paragraphs composed of three sentences, the last sentence being: "Measures within the competence of security organs and the military police, as well as some command measures are being taken and isolated incidents of attempted robbery in the zone of responsibility of the Pristina Corps are being successfully prevented." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, is this a type of reporting on security issues, issues involving crimes against civilians from the 3rd Army that you are accustomed to?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a standard report; however, I wish to state point 5, security in the army, that is exclusively in the domain of the security administration. That's the institution that deals with that. As for morale, that is in the morale administration. Then also the mobilisation and system-based issues fall within the domain of that administration. That has nothing to do with the operations centre and my own line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Let's briefly discuss your own line of work. If you look at paragraph 23 of your statement, do I understand you correct to be saying that during the war in 1999 Supreme Command orders were not accessible to you in the operations centre, except when they were dealing with issues involving the work of the operations centre? Do you have your statement there before you or do you have paragraph 23 on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that that's the way it is and the statement is correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: -- The operations centre received only excerpts from orders that had to do with it itself, orders to the operations centre arrived through the superior administration, and that is the first administration. Therefore, there was no need for all the reports and other documents to be made available to the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. And am I understanding what you said today -- what you said earlier today to be correct that from the 4th -- I take it the 4th of April the daily combat reports from the formations that were directly subordinate to the Supreme Command did not go to the operations centre because the operations duty team was in a separate location?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct; however, the duty operations team was not at a different location. The centre was in a separate room, and the system of work did not make it possible to work as one did in peacetime. All orders, all reports from subordinate units, or rather, orders vis-a-vis units and reports from subordinate units went through the telegraph centre directly to the administration of the first administration. The first administration was the mainstay for operations and staff activities within the Supreme Command Staff and from this administration reports were sent to the operations duty team. The operations duty team --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I was really interested in is what material had passed through your hands or would have been seen by you as chief of the operations centre. By April of 1999 the reports from the subordinate formations to the Supreme Command would not pass through the -- at the operations centre; that is correct, I take it?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. The operations centre at the time carried out the handover of speech information about sorties by enemy air force, received reports on the consequences of certain activities, and submitted that information to the operations duty team in order to get more complete daily operations reports on the situation in the army for that day. There was a lot of information. On average, every half minute one speech information came in, and all this information was recorded in the operations log of the operations centre, and from there submitted to the operations duty team in order to complete the daily combat report for that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the operations duty team would get the daily combat reports from the 3rd Army, the Pristina Corps, and -- well, let me ask you this: What military formations operational in Kosovo during the conflict were directly subordinated to the Supreme Command, that is, reported directly to the Supreme Command? I take it one was the 3rd Army, another was the Pristina Corps, and I see that in your statement. Were there any other military formations operational in Kosovo that reported directly to the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- during the war then, the operations duty team would get the reports, I take it from your evidence, from the 3rd Army and from the Pristina Corps in respect to events in Kosovo. Were you a part of the operations duty team? I know you were the head or the chief of the operations centre which provided logistics, et cetera, for that team. Were you during the war a member of the operations duty team?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: From time to time, yes, save for four days and then there would be a break of eight to ten days, depending on the obligations involved, and then another four days, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you were not there or not in a position to receive these reports for breaks of up to eight and ten days during the conflict, you are not really in a position, are you, to say what you said in paragraph 27 of your statement - if it could be shown to you - that during the NATO aggression the 3rd Army command did not report in combat or other kind of report on deportations of civilians, mass killings of civilians, rapes, destruction of civilian, religious buildings, or other crimes. Now would not be in a position to say that categorically and unequivocally, would you?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: I assert on the basis of what I saw, and my statement is based on what I had seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Again in paragraph 31 - and maybe I'm asking you something which is pretty much obvious from what you are saying - you say that you have no information about the existence of the Joint Command and the staff for the MUP. That is because you -- well, it is possible that there was information in respect of these bodies, but you would not have seen it?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot make any assertions in that regard. What I can assert is that had there been some other command, if it was a command, it certainly would have been part of the military chain of command and I would have had it on my table at the operations centre as a command that I'm duty-bound to communicate with. I did not have any such thing, not at a single point in time, during the course of the aggression or before or after.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look quickly at P2930.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while it's coming up, could I ask you this, at paragraph 24 of your statement you said that copies of the Geneva Convention were sent to -- may I quote it directly. "Copies of the Geneva Conventions and the instructions for conduct of VJ members in combat actions were made. A copy of these documents was given to each VJ member." When were these copies distributed to each VJ member?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot make any definite assertions in this regard, but these brochures did exist. I had one in my pocket and I'm sure that every soldier got something like that because I remember, I know, that we had this major distribution of such material vis-a-vis the units. I don't remember the time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know how many soldiers there were in the VJ at the time of this - what did you say? - this major distribution?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was the sector for mobilisation that was in charge of that. That was not the line of work of my centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you quickly browse the front page you will see that's a combat report from the Pristina Corps of the 31st of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could move to paragraph -- to page 2 in the English and remain on page 1 in B/C/S, focus on paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Paragraph 4 indicates that: "Ministry of the Interior and military territorial units are controlling the territory and channelling the Siptar refugees to the Republic of Albania. There were no particular incidents." Did you see reports of this nature of the MUP and the VJ channelling people to a foreign country, to Albania?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Reports from the MUP I could not see because we did not have any communication with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did you see Pristina Corps reports that documented this type of activity?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: If this report went through the operations centre, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I understand your answer. Did you or do you have a recollection of seeing reports from the Pristina Corps documenting the channelling of civilians across the border? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I see that here, in this document, and I repeat, I don't see the last page of the report because that would confirm whether it went through the operations centre. I don't know whether this is a document that was in the operations centre. I really have no doubts, but it is a stamp that verifies that on the last page. I see this information, and I believe that this is activity that the commander of the 3rd Army -- of the Pristina Corps reports about to his superior command as to what is going on in his territory. I cannot into the core of the matter regarding refugees, the need to re-channel, and so on, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivkovic -- sorry, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the second page should be shown to the witness because it seems to me that Mr. Stamp is misleading him a bit, but I don't want to make any comments. Let him have a look at the other page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will have your chance to deal with that in re-examination. Mr. Ivkovic, one of the biggest issues in Kosovo in -- at the end of March 1999 was refugees and the movement of Albanians towards the Republic of Albania. And you're being asked what is a very important question in this trial whether you, who was in receipt -- who were in receipt of reports recollect receiving reports of the MUP and the military territorial units channelling refugees proceeding to the border. Are you saying you have no recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I had no occasion to see any MUP reports simply there were none to be had in the operations centre. I saw the reports of the command of the 3rd Army and that of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivkovic, you know that we're not talking about report of the MUP. What you have in front of you is a combat report of the Pristina Corps. So the question you're being asked relates to your experience of reporting by the army. Now, are you saying you have no recollection of reports coming to you from other army units that representatives of the Ministry of the Interior and military territorial units were channelling Albanian refugees to the border?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure what my word counts for here, but I didn't process these reports myself. These reports would reach us and we would forward them immediately to the duty operations team in peace and wartime alike. They were the ones who were processing these reports, based on which they produced daily combat reports in wartime and daily reports in peacetime. I personally was involved in the drafting of a report only when I was on shift at the command post, on duty during the actual combat operations. As for this report, I really can't say. I saw the last page, I can't see the stamp, I can't see that it was rubber-stamped by the operations centre, I can't see the incoming stamp. It would have been impossible for it to reach the centre without being recorded as an incoming document, and the fact is I can't see the stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now perhaps you would answer my question. I'm not asking you about anything beyond your own personal experience. You've already told us you were not always on duty and nobody can be 24 hours a day, every day of the month. I simply want to know whether you're saying you have no recollection at all of reports of this nature about the channelling of refugees towards the border; is that your position, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't confirm this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, do you have any recollection or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you - and this is a slightly different question - do you have any recollection of any orders emanating from the Supreme Command to the subordinate units in Kosovo about how to deal with refugees?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can't remember a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I -- to save some time I won't, unless it's insisted upon, show you the document. But we have evidence before us of briefing to the chief of the Supreme Command of the 3rd of April, 1999, and for the record that's 3D721, in which at page 1 of that briefing the chief of the Supreme Command, Major-General Krga, refers to a claim that there are 500 refugees and proposes that refugee check-point be set-up. Are you aware, sir, of any orders or directives from the Supreme Command during the war in respect to setting up check-points for refugees?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the figure you've quoted accurate, 500 refugees?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I believe -- I understand where Mr. Stamp is citing from, but it says "punk" in Serbian, it is not a check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think we better have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see the notes of the briefing before you. If you look at item 2, six bullet points down, can you read that for us aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you read it, please, Mr. Ivkovic, the sixth bullet point, the one referring to the figure 500.000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "They claim that there are about 500.000 refugees." That's bullet six.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Continue, please. Continue reading, please.

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Bullet seven: "I propose that refugee points be set up."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know what a refugee point is or was at the time?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, if we could move on quickly to another issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We are going to have a break -- we will need to have a break very soon --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Mr. Stamp, unless you're near the end of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I think I would have perhaps 15 minutes remaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ivkovic, we have to have a break at this stage for various reasons, and that will be for half an hour. Would you leave the courtroom, please, with the usher, and we will see you again at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have evidence before the Court that on occasion very senior generals in the VJ, for example, General Andjelkovic and General Dimitrijevic, would complain at collegium meetings that sometimes the reporting up to the Supreme Command and to the General Staff from the formation in Kosovo was not accurate. Did you know of these complaints?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I take it, therefore, that you do not -- you are not aware of any measures, any orders or measures sent down from the Supreme Command in respect to rectifying the problem arising from accuracy -- or inaccuracy of the reports from these units?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: In that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is -- you agree with what I said, that you don't --

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not attend a single meeting of the collegium. That wasn't my job --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have any knowledge of such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look at 3D -- and I'm moving on to something else. Can we look at 3D723.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: From the front page which is before you, you can see it is a briefing to the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command of the 5th of April, 1999, and if we go to page 4 in the B/C/S, which is also page 4 in English, we have there that the chief of the Supreme Command says, and this is in the middle of the page, he says: "Unusual incidents that occurred outside of combat, they should undergo the same procedure as in peacetime. Measures against perpetrators should be undertaken immediately. Colonel Ivkovic must immediately write up a warning. All losses must be analysed from the perspective of command errors." Do you recall what he was referring to and what your responsibility or what you were ordered to do?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what this specific case is about, but the operations centre was reporting about unusual developments. Everything that happens outside combat itself is termed an unusual development in this case. Anything that happens in the course of combat is not unusual, for example, people getting killed or wounded. But, for example, wilful abandonment of positions, traffic accidents causing death or injury, outside combat, this would constitute an unusual event. It was in this sense that I wrote certain orders, warning about the need to take measures to prevent any unusual events and developments like these occurring which might have serious consequences. I don't know what specific order you're referring to here. There was several such orders. Whenever there was something out of the ordinary happening, we did our best to remind our units of their responsibility to prevent these, and we also wanted to have these reported on pursuant to the rules on unusual developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Your centre was an organizational unit of the first operations administration, but I see from your statement in paragraph 5 so let me move on to the question I want to ask you.

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In that capacity or in any capacity, did you see any document issued by the General Staff referring to the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not see such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a document and ask you a couple questions about it, it's P1487. You have it before you there. It's the top left-hand section it is written there "Supreme Command Staff, staff operations department, operations administration." That is your department?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this is a document signed by the chief of the Supreme Command, General Ojdanic, and you can see it's sent to the 3rd Army command, to the commander personally, dated the 17th of April, 1999. And he has there a link to Kosovo and Metohija Joint Command order, strictly confidential number 455-148 of 15th of April, 1999. And the general goes on to make some suggestions. Having seen that, can you remember seeing any order that referred to the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I extend that question a little and ask if you ever saw any document in which the words "Joint Command" were used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I take it from that answer, you would not know or you do not know about this Joint Command order strictly confidential number 455-148 -- 455-148, you do not know about that, do you?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The answer to your last -- to my last question was perhaps not -- perhaps not clearly translated, perhaps it was. I'll ask you the question again. Did you ever see any document in which the words "Joint Command" were used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have nothing further in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivkovic, could you look, please, at your statement. Do you actually have a hard copy of your statement there or do we have to put it on the screen? Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the screen then paragraph 13 which is on page 3 of the statement. In that paragraph you talk about reports of the commands of the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps making no mention of organized crimes. When you were answering questions put by Mr. Ackerman, I got the impression that this is material which you say wasn't reported to you anyway. Have I misunderstood that?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: I must point one thing out. From the 4th of April onwards, not a single report was submitted by the operations centre to the Supreme Command Staff. This went straight from the communications centre to the administration and then to the operations -- duty operations team, and that is why my statement reflects just that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In paragraph 13, what reports of the commands of the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Those that had reached the operations centre by that time, and then the operations centre duly submitted them or forwarded them to the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is that all prior to the 4th of April?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: Prior to the 4th of April, that much is certain, but in part I also read reports later on when I was on duty. And I couldn't find anything about organized crime. All I found was about individual cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But a number of times in answering Mr. Ackerman you said that this was not your area of responsibility, and then you were referring to the judicial and prosecutor's reports.

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. Indeed, this wasn't my area of responsibility, it wasn't my job to monitor that or do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman, was there something you wanted to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was raised by Mr. Stamp in explaining to you what it is that I would like to go into would I think unfairly telegraph to the witness what it is I would like him to answer in response to a question I might ask, so I don't know quite how to handle it. I think maybe the easiest way for me to handle it is simply -- if it is appropriate for me to point out to you what I would have presented to the witness because his answer is not going to be all that important to it anyhow. It's just a matter of a couple of documents. And I think it's important, however, to do that now so that a lingering misapprehension doesn't carry forward for days and days until I can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just go ahead and ask the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, just go ahead and tell us what you want to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that one document I showed him, the report that contained the criminal report, Mr. Stamp pointed out that that was contained under the heading: "Army manpower levels."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it was. And I suggest to you that they were a clerical error, that it should have been under the previous heading, which is: "Situation and activities in army units," and I have a number of those reports where it in fact -- that's where it does appear, that would be the appropriate place for it, and that was just an anomaly of the one I chose to use today. Those have all been admitted in evidence so they're available for Your Honours to look at. 4D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give us the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can give some, 4D276 and 4D280, both of those show it under: "Situation and activities in army units."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's helpful. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ackerman showed you a document 4D275. This is a combat report of the 3rd Army dated the 2nd of February, 1999. Later on he asked you whether you had noticed -- the 2nd of April, 1999. And later he asked you whether General Pavkovic's reports had anything to do with the activities of the Tribunal and the OTP and were those almost routinely dropped from the reports that were sent to the supreme commander. Can you please look at 3D807.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, there's something tragically wrong with interpretation. I don't think Mr. Visnjic asked if this had anything with activities of the Tribunal and the OTP. That's what it says in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should be tribunal and the prosecutor or the courts and the prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The plural and the singular are identical in the B/C/S, therefore it was impossible to tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you're talking about the military courts and the military prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- In relation to events in Kosovo; you're not talking about this Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Or this OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you have the document in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Anyway, I think I have wrong document. I withdraw questions. [Interpretation] Can we please have P2930.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, Mr. Stamp asked you some questions about this exhibit. Can you please tell us who issued this document?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: I can only assume, it was probably the forward command post or some command group that the Pristina Corps sent out on a mission. They are now reporting back to their own command about this. This is a corps document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us who it was sent to?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: As it reads, to the command of the Pristina Corps, operations centre, Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the next page, page 2. Let's look at the signature.

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the leader of the command group Colonel Ljubomir Pesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, back at the operations centre did you receive any reports from subordinate units, those subordinate to the Pristina Corps, I mean?

utterances.speaker: STANISA IVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, none, only from the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we finally tracked down the right number for the document that I referred to earlier on, the one that Mr. Ackerman asked you about, it's 4D275, dated the 2nd of February, 1999. After that there was a question by Mr. Ackerman -- I'm sorry, another slip of the tongue on my part. It's 4D275, dated the 2nd of April, 1999. I will now go back to Mr. Ackerman's question about the substance of the combat report of the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 3D808. Your Honours, we don't have a translation of this document. It has not been translated yet. It belongs to an entire set of documents that remain untranslated, but with the exception of the title I would like to ask the interpreters to interpret just a single sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, not having this in a language that I can read, I think it's unfair for it to be brought up at this point when I am not in any kind of position to deal with it in case I need to. So I would object to it being brought up until there's a translation. We can't keep going on without translations like this because it absolutely impairs the ability of cross-examiners or the Judges to deal with these documents. You can't read it, there might be something in there that you would like to ask about. I just think it's unfair; they should be translated before they're used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the reason for the problem in this case, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem, you mean why the document has not been translated yet? There's an entire set of documents, Your Honour, combat reports from the Supreme Command Staff. The CLSS came back to us: We were under a lot of pressure. They stopped the translation process at one point, and now we are getting them translated as we speak, but these documents were on our exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you've had them for some considerable time and we have asked you to prioritize the arrangements for translation and we know you've done pretty well, but this does present a difficulty. It's a re-examination. Is this an absolutely essential question that you have to pose here or is it something that can be dealt with by submissions once the document has been translated? Because a lot of your questions in re-examination are not really matters that need to be presented through evidence from a witness in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't think that should be a problem. We'll be hearing a witness next week who will be a good witness for the introduction of that document. I hope that by such time the document will have been translated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll sustain the objection in light of that and you should move to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No, I don't have further question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivkovic, that brings your evidence to an end. Thank you for coming to give evidence. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before we proceed I would like to deal with the issue of the expert reports of Radinovic and Simunovic. This is perhaps an example of the Trial Chamber's indulgence in generosity coming back to haunt it. What we'll do, Mr. Hannis, in relation to Radinovic is allow you until the 15th of October to take the steps you consider appropriate under Rule 94 bis (B). We would then expect you to discuss with Mr. Visnjic whether you have ongoing difficulties about dealing with Radinovic the witness at that point and whether he should then be heard after General Ojdanic. We recognise that one of the points you made to us was that you needed to see this to prepare properly to cross-examine Mr. Ojdanic, but I think there's a difference between that and being able to deal with the report itself with the witness himself. So we would hope that you could agree on how you're going to do it. If we have to resolve the order of events, we will resolve it, but having heard Mr. Visnjic yesterday, it's likely that you'll get your way on that. If you wish more time to prepare for Radinovic, then he would have to lead Mr. Ojdanic before he led that evidence. Now, we'll put this -- the bare bones of this order in writing later today for the avoidance of any doubt. So far as Simunovic is concerned, in the hope of assisting you to concentrate on Radinovic and since Simunovic is so far down the line, what we'll do there is extend the deadline for Rule 94 bis (B) to the 16th of November, by which time we'll be beyond Radinovic and into other territory in the case. Now, Mr. Visnjic, in light of the possibility that there's going to be some sort of gap it may be you don't fill next week, for example, in light of all this and because Radinovic would not be giving evidence at that stage, we need a little guidance from you on timing. How long is it you envisage him giving evidence in chief for?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're asking me about Radinovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Only one hour I believe, not more than one hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be then - and obviously you may come to a different arrangement with Mr. Hannis - but it may be that the most helpful way of dealing with this is for Mr. Ojdanic to give evidence before Radinovic, since we know that his evidence will be lengthy. And it may be also that you would consider, please, trying to confine the evidence of Mr. Ojdanic to the week beginning the 15th -- well, we won't be actually sitting on the 15th, so that would be the four days from the 16th of October. All we can do is ask you to consider doing that, consider tailoring his evidence to fit that time-scale in the interests of every accused and the Prosecution involved in this case. Now, we can proceed to your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our next is Spasoje Mucibabic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mucibabic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You'll now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us briefly something about your military career, what posts you held and what schools you completed?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC
utterances.text: I joined the army on the 1st of September, 1966. I came to the military academy of the land forces the 23rd class, and I completed the academy on the 20th of July, 1970, at the top of my class with straight A stars, straight 10s. This is a generation that had several witnesses here --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, we don't have much time. We really cannot go into this entire history. Tell me, after you completed the academy, tell us what your major posts were.

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC
utterances.text: I focused on education in my career. In addition to that, I was in command in the field of atomic, biological, chemical defence. At the end of my career I was in the General Staff too, in the analysis organs. I ended my career as a professor and head of the top military school, the National Defence school.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You were retired in what rank?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC
utterances.text: I was retired on the 12th of April, 2004, as major-general and as a full professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What duties did you discharge during the bombing in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC
utterances.text: During the aggression in 1999 as a member of the operations administration, I was chief of a department. I discharged that duty, or rather, I shared that duty with Colonel Dragan Paskas.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us where you were located physically, this department of yours, or rather, this administration where you worked during the course of the bombing, that is?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC
utterances.text: The operations administration, according to wartime establishment, during the aggression was located at the command post, and that is where we were invariably during the stage of our work. During the stage of our rest, we would sometimes go outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the command post where you were, can you tell us how the work of your administration was organized?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC
utterances.text: It's a complicated question. An answer would be long. Principles of command and control at strategic level guided us, and all of this functioned flawlessly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, where you were, the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command now, did he organize, or rather, did he have evening meetings?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC
utterances.text: Yes, these were not evening meetings. These were regular, daily briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We have heard a number of witnesses here testifying about various meetings that were organized by the Supreme Command Staff and the General Staff. How would you describe the difference between a collegium meeting and these meetings that you referred to as briefings and was there any difference at all?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't refer to these as briefings myself. This is a matter of military doctrine. You call it a meeting, I call it a briefing. This is military-speak. As for the differences, I did not attend any collegium meetings because I was not a member of the collegium, not ever. However, based on its responsibilities and duties, the collegium is supposed to discuss all issues to do with command and control. Briefings, on the other hand, normally serve a particular purpose, especially during combat operations, the objective being to consider previous events, overall developments, problems, and eventually proposals are made as to how to deal with certain problems and continue combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, when were these briefings normally held?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC
utterances.text: As a rule, the briefings took place in the evening, normally between 1800 hours and 1900 hours, depending on the operative situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Where were these held physically, in which room?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC
utterances.text: In the operations room of the Supreme Command physically.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What was your responsibility in relation to these briefings?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC
utterances.text: My responsibility as well as that of my colleague, Colonel Paskas, and we were at the third level in terms of rank and responsibility under the Chief of the General Staff, as we soldiers call it, our responsibility was below the line. It was about making sure the conditions were as good as possible for the briefing, and this also entailed keeping minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you say making sure the conditions were as good as possible for the briefing, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC
utterances.text: Given the type of the facility being used, the operations room had a number of different uses. There were other daily activities occurring there. This was about the work regimen in wartime. One needed to prepare all these things, and this implied that the room needed to be set up, the conditions, tickets, seats, making sure the room wasn't musty and the air wasn't stale, and everything else that wartime conditions normally imply.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You said you were one of the persons in charge of the minutes, of taking minutes. What sort of document were you using for these minutes?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC
utterances.text: I was using a minutes notebook, a special notebook for minutes, which was a combat report of the operative administration.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Combat document, not a combat report, correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, who issued you the order to keep minutes?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC
utterances.text: This is envisaged in the description of the responsibilities of my department, the department in which I was working with Colonel Paskas. It was in the nature of things that we should be in charge. The specific order came from our superior officer, and at the time this was General Obradovic. I believe he appeared before this Trial Chamber in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, while you were working at the command post -- first of all, which rank did you hold at the time?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC
utterances.text: I was a colonel back then. I had been a professional soldier for nine years. I had been a colonel for nine years.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And what was Paskas's rank at the time?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC
utterances.text: He was a colonel as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that both you and Colonel Paskas at the time were department heads. Is my understanding correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC
utterances.text: Yes. In practical terms we were the heads of a single department. We took turns, but I had spent a much longer time in the operative administration, so I was chief and he was deputy chief technically speaking, although we were on an equal footing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So how did you take turns, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC
utterances.text: Of course I remember. We had shifts, and these shifts were based on the operative situation that prevailed. There was a plan, normally four- to six-day shifts, depending on the situation and sometimes the shifts would be longer or shorter, as I said, depending on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let's leave aside the issue of taking minutes. What was your principal responsibility there?

utterances.speaker: SPASOJE MUCIBABIC
utterances.text: My principal responsibility was the operative function, preparing, organizing, and carrying through the operative function at the command post of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. In military-speak, in military doctrine this is clearly defined. In order to explain this I would require some more time. If you are prepared for this, I would be happy to explain but it might take some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Tell us what that means. We don't need to know the details, just tell us the general nature of what you did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The nature was this: Preparation implied preparing manpower and equipment for optimal work; organizing entailed the optimal deployment of manpower and equipment and making sure that the functioning, too, was optimal. The execution itself was a result of these two prerequisites and worked in keeping with the rules, the rules that we had and also depending on the situation that prevailed or any orders received from our superior officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this what I would understand as logistics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Please, logistics for us is a separate thing, it is exceptionally important. During the aggression logistics was termed "rear security." This was an operative function of the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Visnjic, we will have to call it a day at this point today and resume with a very brief and simple explanation of the job tomorrow morning -- or tomorrow afternoon in fact; regrettably that's still the case. Mr. Mucibabic, we have to terminate the hearing today at this point because there are other cases in this courtroom in the afternoon; that means you have to return here tomorrow to continue your evidence, that will be at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon. Between now and then it's vital that you should have no discussion, no communication, with anyone at all about the evidence in this case. You can communicate on any other subject, but you must not with any person whatsoever discuss the evidence. Now would you please leave the courtroom with the usher and return here for 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank the Chamber for informing me about this. This is the first time I find myself facing a situation such as this, and I will try to do as you have told me to do. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Try -- trying's not enough, Mr. Mucibabic. Trying is not good enough, you just have to do it, it's as simple as that. So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Assistant implementation of orders, that is what we do in the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Please leave the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 28th day of September, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.20 p.m.,
